novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Snijders RJM, Nicolaides KH. UOG 1994;4:34-48
novedades.texto: GA is estimated with the Snijders and Nicolaides (1994) equation. The rule TCD (mm) ≈ GA (weeks) holds only up to 20–21 wk. TCD is little affected by growth restriction, but it may be reduced in severe FGR: do not use it alone to date a small fetus (Snijders 1994; Vinkesteijn 2000). Enter the GA by LMP or early scan to obtain the centile. TCD <5th centile for GA: suspected cerebellar hypoplasia; refer to Fetal Medicine and rule out Dandy-Walker and other CNS malformations. TCD >95th centile: review dating.

novedades.titulo: Fetal structural morphology — 7 systems (20-24 week scan)
novedades.fuentes: ISUOG Practice Guidelines (2020/2023) — CNS, face, heart · Paladini & Volpe (2018) · Jeanty P et al. 1982/1984 · Mayden KL et al. 1982 · Sukonpan K, Phupong V 2008 · Burns NS et al. 2013 · Corteville JE et al. 1991/1992 · FMF/Nicolaides · CDHSG / Jani et al. 2007
novedades.texto: Structured system-by-system checklist, 18-24 weeks, immediately after the 2nd-trimester FMF screening. CNS: cavum septum pellucidum (absent ⚠️), symmetric thalami, cranial shape ("lemon"/"strawberry" sign ⚠️), lateral ventricular atrium (normal <10mm · mild 10-15mm · severe >15mm, measured at the level of the choroid plexus glomus), cisterna magna (normal 3.0-10.0mm; <2-3mm obliterated, >10mm mega cisterna magna), 2T nuchal fold (valid 15.0-20.6 wk, normal <6.0mm), banana sign, and cerebellar vermis agenesis. An obliterated cisterna magna plus a banana sign point toward open spina bifida — correlate with the spine. Face: orbits, nose, maxilla, palate (retronasal coronal view), and upper lip. Orbital diameters (axial view with both lenses): IOD, interocular distance from inner edge to inner edge, and BOD, binocular distance from outer edge to outer edge. IOD <5th centile for GA: hypotelorism; IOD >95th centile: hypertelorism (ISUOG). Reference medians (Sukonpan 2008): IOD 20 wk ≈13 · 24 ≈15 · 28 ≈17 mm; BOD 20 wk ≈31 · 24 ≈38 · 28 ≈44 mm. The calculator compares with weekly 5th–95th centiles. Spine: bony continuity on longitudinal + axial views, and intact overlying skin. Chest and heart (+ CDH): situs, 4-chamber view, ventricular/atrial symmetry, interventricular septum (VSD), outflow tracts, 3-vessel and trachea view, aortic arch. Cardiothoracic area ratio: normal 0.25-0.33, cardiomegaly >0.35. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: intrathoracic gastric bubble, side (left Bochdalek ~85%), O/E LHR <25% severe · 25-44.9% moderate · ≥45% favorable. Abdomen: stomach (rule out "double bubble" — duodenal atresia, ~30% association with T21), abdominal wall/cord (omphalocele vs. gastroschisis), renal pelvic dilation (<33 wk obstructive >10.0mm; ≥33 wk obstructive >10.0mm with a distinct normal cutoff of <7.0mm), kidneys (uni/bilateral agenesis, multicystic dysplasia), single umbilical artery, 2T/3T megacystis (≥16 wk, pathological if longitudinal diameter > [GA in weeks + 12]mm), and "keyhole sign" (PUV). Limbs: 3 segments per limb (humerus/radius-ulna/hand; femur/tibia-fibula/foot) to avoid missing reduction defects, polydactyly (soft marker for T13/Meckel-Gruber/Bardet-Biedl if isolated), and clubfoot. Placenta, cord, amniotic fluid, cervix: placental location (low-lying <20mm from the internal os) and cord insertion site (marginal "racquet" vs. velamentous — vasa previa risk, confirm with color Doppler).

novedades.texto: PUL: do not treat without ultrasound confirmation; βhCG at 48 h with a minimum rise of 49 % (<1500), 40 % (1500-3000) or 33 % (>3000) (AAFP 2020). Complicated (free fluid, severe pain, instability): emergency surgery + Code Red; salpingectomy is preferred. Tubal ectopic pregnancy — criteria by source Management CaVeSal (calculator) MSPBS 2018 NICE NG126 Expectant β-hCG <1000 and declining, no criteria β-hCG <5000, mass ≤35 mm, fluid ≤300 mL, no heartbeat ≤1000 offer; 1000-1500 consider Methotrexate 50 mg/m² IM β-hCG 1000-<5000, mass <35 mm, no heartbeat β-hCG <6000, mass ≤40 mm <1500 first-line; 1500-5000 either option Surgery ≥5000, mass ≥35 mm, heartbeat or pain Outside criteria; salpingectomy ≥5000, ≥35 mm, heartbeat or pain CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: MSPBS 2018 · NICE NG126 (ectopic pregnancy). Methotrexate follow-up: β-hCG on days 4 and 7; decline ≥15 % → weekly until negative; otherwise, second dose or surgery. Anti-D if Rh(-). Non-tubal ectopics (RCOG GTG 21): cervical → methotrexate; for evacuation, uterine artery embolization or vaginal uterine artery clamping (Zea technique) · cesarean scar → neither expectant management nor systemic methotrexate alone; aspiration or resection · interstitial/cornual → methotrexate or cornual resection · abdominal → early laparoscopy; advanced, laparotomy with the placenta left in situ. Cesarean scar ectopic pregnancy: stepwise management Management by scenario Scenario Management Hemodynamic instability, suspected uterine rupture, hemoperitoneum or active bleeding Urgent surgery and Code Red Vial type I (toward the cavity) with residual myometrium >2 mm and βhCG <5000 mIU/mL Ultrasound-guided intragestational methotrexate, alone or combined (GRADE 2C); alternative: ultrasound-guided aspiration Type I with myometrium >2 mm and βhCG 5000 to 30,000 mIU/mL Hysteroscopy: visualize the sac with a 5 mm diagnostic hysteroscope and resect with a resectoscope (success 87.4%, complications 4.1%) Vial type II (toward bladder or serosa), myometrium ≤2 mm or βhCG >30,000 One-step laparoscopic resection (10 steps: bladder dissection, preventive hemostasis, hysterotomy, evacuation, niche excision and lower segment repair) or vaginal resection Chooses to continue the pregnancy Cesarean delivery between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks (GRADE 1C) In all cases: no expectant management (GRADE 1B), no sharp curettage alone (2C) and no systemic methotrexate alone (1C). At discharge, counsel on the risks of another pregnancy and offer long-acting or permanent contraception (1C). After methotrexate, wait 6 months before a new pregnancy. There is no universal residual myometrium cutoff (<2 or <3 mm are used). Reported efficacy and complications (SMFM #63, case series) Method Patients Efficacy Complications Expectant management 41 41.5% 53.7% Systemic methotrexate 339 75% 13% Needle aspiration + systemic methotrexate 148 84.5% 15.5% Curettage (D&C) 243 48% 21% Hysteroscopy 95 83% 3.2% Transvaginal resection 118 >99% 0.9% Embolization + curettage 295 93.6% 3.4% Laparoscopy 69 97.1% 0% Local methotrexate 74 64.9% 4.1% High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) 16 100% 0% Cited alternatives: in a series of 154 cases, surgery (laparoscopy, hysteroscopy or combined) cured 97.9%, HIFU followed by curettage 70.4% and embolization followed by curettage 43.7%; HIFU worked best under 55 days and with a sac smaller than 30 mm. novedades.texto: FIGO 2019 clinical classification Grade Intraoperative finding 1 Adherent placenta (creta): no myometrial invasion 2 Increta: myometrial invasion, without reaching the serosa 3a Percreta limited to the uterine serosa 3b Percreta with bladder invasion 3c Percreta with invasion of other pelvic tissues or organs Risk of placenta accreta spectrum with placenta previa according to number of cesarean deliveries (Silver 2006) Cesarean delivery 1ª 2ª 3ª 4ª ≥5ª Risk of PAS 3% 11% 40% 61% 67% Without placenta previa, risk ranges from 0.24% to 6.74% according to the number of cesarean deliveries. Ultrasound signs (ISUOG 2016): loss of the retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, myometrial thinning <1 mm, disruption of the bladder line, placental bulge, focal exophytic mass; Doppler: uterovesical or subplacental hypervascularity and bridging vessels. Antenatal diagnosis (WAPM/PMF 2026): after a previous cesarean, early transvaginal ultrasound to rule out cesarean scar pregnancy (a potential precursor of PAS); in the 2nd-3rd trimester, combined transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound; MRI is only complementary (inconclusive ultrasound, non-anterior or non-previa placenta). If suspected, refer to a perinatal center with a multidisciplinary team. Timing of scheduled cesarean delivery (comparison of sources) Source Window ACOG/SMFM Obstetric Care Consensus No. 7 (2018) 34+0 to 35+6 weeks RCOG Green-top 27a (5th ed., 2026) 35+0 to 36+6 weeks, without risk factors for preterm birth WAPM/PMF (2026) Individualize according to bleeding, suspected invasion and center resources Management: level III-IV center with a multidisciplinary team and blood bank; corticosteroids if <37 weeks; tranexamic acid at onset; uterine incision away from the placenta and cesarean hysterectomy with the placenta in situ (do not attempt placental separation). Activate Code Red in the event of bleeding. Topographic classification of PAS It classifies the lesion by the affected uterine wall and its relation to the vesicouterine fold; each type has its own arterial pedicles, which define vascular control and treatment. On ultrasound, with a half-full bladder, a line perpendicular to the midpoint of the posterior bladder wall separates upper lesions (sector S1) from lower lesions (sector S2). Final staging is intraoperative. Topographic classification of PAS and proposed treatment Type Location Main blood supply Vascular control Proposed treatment 0 Upper anterior; the placenta detaches Uterine None One-step conservative surgery (OSCS) 1 Upper anterior; the placenta does not detach Uterine, superior vesical branches Dissection and ligation of newly formed vessels OSCS 2U Upper lateral (parametrial) Obturator, internal iliac collaterals, uterine Dissection and ligation of newly formed vessels OSCS if there is enough healthy caudal tissue 2L Lower lateral (parametrial) Internal iliac collaterals, cervical, vaginal Infrarenal aortic occlusion or temporary occlusion of both common iliacs Total hysterectomy after ureteral tunneling 3 Lower anterior Superior and inferior vesical, uterine, cervical, vaginal Infrarenal aortic occlusion or temporary occlusion of both common iliacs OSCS or total hysterectomy 4 Lower anterior with vesicouterine fibrosis Same as type 3 Same as type 3 Modified subtotal hysterectomy (MSTH) 5U Upper posterior Uterine, ovarian, vicarious flow from the inferior mesenteric Uterine artery ligation OSCS 5L Lower posterior Uterine, anterior rectal collaterals Collateral ligation; aortic occlusion? Total hysterectomy Criteria for one-step conservative surgery (OSCS): bladder separable from the uterus, 2 cm or more of healthy myometrium below the affected area and involvement of less than 50% of the uterine circumference in the axial plane, with no low parametrial involvement. The placenta and the invaded myometrium are resected together, en bloc, and the uterus is reconstructed. Only in trained centers with a multidisciplinary team. Modified subtotal hysterectomy (type 4): retrovesical dissection stops where it can no longer continue, a subtotal hysterectomy is performed, the placenta is removed from the stump under proximal aortic control and compression sutures are placed on the anterior and posterior stump walls. Alternatives cited and not recommended by the source: total hysterectomy with partial bladder resection, leaving part of the uterus attached to the bladder, or leaving the placenta in situ. Ward maneuver (anterior placenta previa): with prenatal mapping of the nearest placental edge, a segmental hysterotomy through the myometrium only, controlled manual separation toward that edge, rupture of membranes, exteriorization of the detached edge and fetal extraction without cutting the placenta. In PAS it is done 1-2 cm above the abnormal area, after ruling out types 2L and 4 at staging. Protocol of a referral center (Hospital Bertha Calderón Roque, Nicaragua): referral to the national center at 32-33 weeks; birth with PAS at 35-36; total occlusive placenta previa without PAS or scar dehiscence, at 37; cardiovascular and pre-anesthetic assessment at 33-34; blood products (red cells, plasma, cryoprecipitate, platelets) and a multidisciplinary team; cystoscopy and ureteral catheters not routine. This is one center's experience, not a guideline. In that hospital, prenatal diagnosis was associated with fewer transfusions (56.9% vs 96.1%); prenatal diagnostic failures were frequent. Errors that cost blood: pulling on or trying to remove an adherent placenta (the most critical error); hysterotomy over the placental bed; blind or blunt vesicouterine dissection without careful dissection of the newly formed vessels; omitting proximal vascular control before hysterectomy or conservative surgery. Avoidable factors: underestimating blood loss, inadequate transfusion and delay in lifesaving surgery. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Nieto-Calvache AJ et al. novedades.texto: Intrauterine balloon tamponade devices (same principle: hydrostatic pressure) Device Characteristic Bakri Obstetric-specific design; up to 500 mL Ellavi Less expensive; similar design to Bakri Condom + Foley/Nelaton catheter Low-cost adaptation for resource-limited settings Rusch catheter Adapted hydrostatic balloon Sengstaken-Blakemore Double balloon (gastric + esophageal); designed for esophageal varices and adapted for uterine tamponade Uterine compression sutures Technique Particularity B-Lynch Classic, “suspender” suture; requires open hysterotomy Hayman Simplified modification; does not require hysterotomy (uterus closed) Pereira Multiple transverse and vertical sutures; closed uterus Ho-Cho Multiple square sutures; particularly indicated for placenta accreta Uterine sandwich Simultaneous intrauterine balloon + external compression suture (B-Lynch + Bakri) Suture for compression sutures: absorbable (chromic catgut or polyglactin 910), No. 1 or No. 2, on a curved needle (the most used). In a systematic review of 76 articles, uterine preservation did not differ between No. 1 and No. 2 (92.8% vs 94.2%); the 4 uterine necroses reported (0.67%) occurred with No. 1 sutures and none with No. 2. Given the heterogeneity of the cases, there is no evidence that one suture is superior: this is guidance, not a directive. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Matsuzaki S et al. BMC Surg 2019;19:196. Quality of the evidence: an updated systematic review (31 studies, 2014-2025) reports 73.9% to 100% efficacy for compression sutures, but almost all evidence comes from uncontrolled case series, Asian tertiary centers and cesarean deliveries; there is no clear hierarchy among techniques and outcomes depend on bleeding severity and case complexity. Newer techniques with removable sutures aim at fewer complications; data on later fertility are encouraging but insufficient. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Ursache A et al. Med Sci (Basel) 2026;14(6):619. Uterine vascular sectors (S1 / S2 / S3) Sector Blood supply Most frequent cause Targeted control S1 · body and fundus Uterine artery; minor contribution from the ovarian artery Atony (uterine hypotonia) Sutures compressing the body (B-Lynch, Hayman, Pereira), uterine artery ligation or embolization, intrauterine balloon S2 · lower segment and cervix Colpouterine arteries (uterine, vesical and vaginal branches) Placenta previa and accreta spectrum; segment dehiscence Low sutures compressing the segment (B-Lynch 2, Ho-Cho) after bladder mobilization, colpouterine artery ligation, vaginal balloon. Uterine artery ligation does not control lower-segment bleeding S3 · middle and upper thirds of the vagina Vaginal arteries, branches of the internal pudendal Tears (precipitous labor, compound presentation, fundal pressure) Exposure of the outer vaginal wall through the prevesical space (Retzius) Uterine tourniquet (primary hemostasis): with the uterus exteriorized, the assistant pulls it upward and the surgeon places a sterile latex glove around the lowest portion of the uterus, ideally at the upper third of the vagina, including the broad ligaments and ovaries, and ties it with maximum traction, below the bleeding site. It does not treat the cause: it limits blood loss while definitive control is applied (secondary hemostasis). Another immediate measure is manual compression of the infrarenal aorta. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Nieto-Calvache AJ et al., FIGO Committee on Childbirth and PPH. Int J Gynaecol Obstet 2025;168(3):987-998 · Nieto-Calvache AJ et al. Int J Gynaecol Obstet 2024;164(1):345-347. Hemorrhage during and after cesarean delivery Causes specific to cesarean delivery: unintended extension of the hysterotomy, uterine vascular pedicle injury, cervical and parametrial injuries, broad ligament injuries, incisions in the uterine body, vesicouterine separation, transplacental hysterotomy, wound hematoma and bleeding from adhesions. These add to the causes shared with vaginal birth: atony, genital trauma, retained placenta and coagulopathy. Persistent hemorrhage at cesarean: conservative surgical escalation Step Action If it persists 1 Bilateral uterine artery ligation or Tsirulnikov triple ligation (uterine arteries, round ligaments and utero-ovarian ligaments) Step 2 2 Uterine compression suture (B-Lynch, Cho) Step 3 3 Bilateral internal iliac artery ligation, only if mastered by the surgical team Step 4 4 Peripartum hysterectomy; abdominal packing if life-threatening hemorrhage persists — Unstable If hemodynamically unstable at any step, go directly to hysterectomy — In parallel: oxygen, prevention of hypothermia, fluid resuscitation, serial blood tests (blood count, coagulation, fibrinogen), red cells, fresh frozen plasma, fibrinogen, general anesthesia and vasopressors as needed. Intrauterine balloons and vacuum devices have not been sufficiently evaluated during cesarean: they may buy time until surgical control. Embolization takes time and is feasible only in stable women with slow bleeding. Delayed hemorrhage after cesarean: bleeding may stay in the abdomen or retroperitoneum, with no vaginal bleeding and no fluid on ultrasound. Any clinical deterioration in the hours after cesarean should raise suspicion of hemorrhage. Relaparotomy without delay is the standard for diagnosis and treatment. Complex cesarean in 3 steps: 1) access to the pelvis when there are extensive adhesions between the uterus and other organs or vessels (paramedian access); 2) bladder dissection and mobilization to expose the lower segment, needed for dehiscence or bleeding; 3) choice of the control strategy according to the bleeding vascular sector. Choice of hysterotomy by scenario Scenario Technique to consider Reason Elective term cesarean, cephalic Low transverse (Kerr) Lower morbidity and better scar 28 weeks, breech, poorly formed segment Low vertical or classical, according to the segment and space Atraumatic extraction Transverse lie, back down Vertical (classical) Wide access for extraction Deeply impacted head in second stage Low transverse, with possible J or inverted-T extension Enlarge the space without traumatic maneuvers Anterior placenta previa or suspected accreta Hysterotomy away from the placenta: upper transverse, classical or fundal Avoid cutting through the placenta Large fibroid in the anterior lower segment Upper transverse, classical or posterior, according to anatomy Avoid incising the fibroid Repeat cesarean with severe vesicouterine adhesions According to access; may require a vertical incision Avoid bladder injury Extreme macrosomia Wide low transverse or vertical, according to presentation and anatomy Avoid traumatic extensions Advantages and risks of each hysterotomy technique Technique Advantage Risk Low transverse Less bleeding, simple repair, lower later rupture risk Lateral or cervical extensions if too low or poorly extended Upper transverse (upper segment) Avoids an anterior placenta or a fibroid in the segment Cuts contractile myometrium: changes the risk in later pregnancies Low vertical Eases some extractions Extension toward the bladder, cervix or upper segment Classical vertical Wide access, useful with unfavorable anatomy More bleeding and higher rupture risk in future pregnancies J-shaped Enlarges the space toward one side Injury to uterine branches, hemorrhage, complex scar U-shaped or inverted T Quickly enlarges the extraction space Complex scar; harder repair; contraindicates later labor Fundal or posterior Avoids an anterior placenta or compromised structures Exceptional technique, more complex, with little comparative evidence Uterine scar and the next pregnancy Scar Later vaginal birth Uterine rupture Low transverse Generally a candidate 0.5 to 0.9% Low vertical limited to the lower segment Selected candidate Similar to low transverse Classical, T or J, extension to the upper segment Contraindicated; planned cesarean 4 to 9% Upper transverse, fundal or posterior Generally contraindicated No solid estimates Management depends on the real extent of the incision: not every T or J extension carries the same risk; what matters is whether it involves the contractile upper segment. Whenever possible, preserve the low transverse incision, without sacrificing fetal safety. The alternatives in this table are those cited by the sources; the choice belongs to the surgical team. Int J Gynaecol Obstet 2025;168(3):987-998 · Nunes I et al., FIGO. Int J Gynaecol Obstet 2023;163(Suppl 2):21-33 · ACOG Practice Bulletin 205. Obstet Gynecol 2019;133(2):e110-e127. Cesarean hysterectomy Ureteral risk zones: infundibulopelvic ligament, below the uterine artery and along its paracervical course to the bladder. Care after cesarean hysterectomy Stage Care Immediate Hemodynamic monitoring, fluid balance and volume, antibiotic prophylaxis, thromboprophylaxis, analgesia, ventilatory support if needed Intermediate Early ambulation, wound care, nutrition, pelvic and abdominal evaluation, psychological support, warning-sign education Late Gynecologic follow-up, pelvic floor, psychological follow-up, sexual health counseling, comorbidities Late complications: vaginal cuff stenosis or granuloma, postcoital bleeding, dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, stress incontinence, overactive bladder, postpartum depression and vesicovaginal fistula. A real series: 82 cesarean hysterectomies (Iran, 2018-2022), with complications in 45: bladder injury 15, ureteral 6, fever 9, surgical site infection 5, hematoma 4, bowel injury 2, reoperation 3 and pulmonary embolism 1; transfusion in 60.95% and accreta as the cause in 58%. Williams Obstetrics, 26th ed. (2022) · Jones HW, Rock JA. Te Linde's Operative Gynecology, 13th ed. (2024). Devascularization and vascular control Technique Particularity Zea (vaginal) Vaginal clamping of the uterine arteries with ring forceps in the lateral parametrium of the cervix; bridging measure while preparing the operating room or addressing the cause. Also useful before evacuating a cervical ectopic pregnancy O'Leary Bilateral ligation of the uterine arteries via laparotomy; first-line conservative surgical option Posadas Selective devascularization: posterior ligation of the uterine arteries and internal tubal arteries, without opening the broad ligament; 96.4% success in 750 cases Tsirulnikov Triple stepwise ligation: round ligaments, utero-ovarian ligaments, and uterine arteries Hypogastric arteries Internal iliac artery ligation; more complex (ureteral and venous risk), reserved for failure of the preceding procedures Arterial embolization Interventional radiology in a hemodynamically stable patient; fertility-preserving CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: INPer — Zea technique · IMSS Clinical Practice Guideline 162 · Ginecol Obstet Méx — Posadas technique · Series of 750 cases. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: WHO 2021 · MSPBS Code Red 2022. Bakri: success rate 79.5-85.9% in systematic reviews; in a meta-analysis of 28 studies, 82% with balloon alone (95% CI 78-86%) and 95% with additional procedures. Lower success after cesarean delivery (69-78%) than after vaginal birth (90%). Sutures: no technique demonstrated clear superiority; efficacy ~75% after failure of medical treatment and ~80% as second-line treatment after failed vascular ligation; risk of synechiae 5-10%. Combined balloon + suture: success rate >91.7% in refractory PPH; avoids hysterectomy in up to 75% of cases that would otherwise require it. Condom/Foley balloon (improvised): WHO 2021 recommends its use only where other treatments, including immediate surgery, are already available. Assembly: 16-18 Foley catheter with the distal tip cut off, inserted into a condom, secured with silk about 5 fingers from the end (without obstructing the lumen); fill with 500 cc of 0.9% normal saline, with vaginal packing to prevent expulsion. In a comparative study of 12 patients (6 per group), the improvised balloon achieved 100% success (6/6), with no complications or associated surgeries, comparable to the SOS Bakri balloon, although time to hemostasis was slightly longer (6.8 vs. 4.6 min, not statistically significant). Source: Jiménez L, Veroes J, Vera M, Colmenares M, Di Muro J, Márquez D. Rev Obstet Ginecol Venez. 2020;80(3):227-235. Comparative reference; the surgical step-by-step is beyond the scope of a quick-reference guide. Included in the Code Red Level 2-3 escalation — in our setting (Paraguay), where Bakri/Ellavi are not always available, the improvised balloon is the usual and clinically equivalent option.

novedades.texto: Pregnancy >20 weeks + 2 BP readings 15 min apart if severe (≥160/110) or 4 h apart if mild (140-159/90-109) + evidence of end-organ damage (clinical: headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, pulmonary edema; laboratory: AST/ALT≥70, LDH≥600, platelets<100,000, bilirubin≥1.2) OR proteinuria (≥300 mg/24h, protein/creatinine ratio≥0.3, albumin/creatinine ratio≥0.8, dipstick≥2+) OR angiogenic tests sFlt1/PlGF>38. Proteinuria is NOT required for the diagnosis of severe preeclampsia. Initial laboratory and proteinuria (ISH 2026): full blood count, urinalysis, creatinine, uric acid and liver enzymes. A positive dipstick should be confirmed with the urine protein-to-creatinine or albumin-to-creatinine ratio. Measure BP with a device validated for pregnancy and preeclampsia. Prevention: calcium 1-2 g/day in all pregnant patients; aspirin 150 mg/day based on risk factors (1 high-risk factor or 2 moderate-risk factors).

novedades.texto: MAP ÷ HR approximates peripheral vascular resistance at the bedside, without echocardiography or noninvasive monitoring. MAP/HR Phenotype Suggested first-line approach >1,4 Hypodynamic: high resistance, normal or low cardiac output; more associated with FGR Calcium channel blocker (nifedipine) 1,1–1,4 Normodynamic Methyldopa <1,1 Hyperdynamic: high output, low resistance Labetalol or methyldopa Guides drug selection only for non-severe hypertension or maintenance therapy. Severe hypertension is treated immediately with the available drug. Some checklists use a single cutoff of 1.4 (≥1.4 hypodynamic). The calculator uses the three ranges from the systematic review. ISH 2026 keeps methyldopa as an alternative (higher risk of postpartum depression) and advises against it after delivery; labetalol and long-acting nifedipine are its first line. Postpartum drugs: any of the recommended antihypertensives, except methyldopa (postpartum depression). Breastfeeding: enalapril, long-acting nifedipine or amlodipine are preferred; beta-blockers may also be used. Data on ARBs are limited. Check each drug's prescribing information. At discharge: these women have a higher risk of hypertension, stroke, ischaemic heart disease and chronic kidney disease. novedades.texto: Code activation: SBP>160 or DBP>110 or eclamptic seizures. Team: Coordinator, Assistant, Circulating Nurse. Post-target monitoring: every 10 min for the 1st hour, every 15 min for the 2nd hour, every 30 min for the 3rd hour, every hour from the 4th hour for an additional 4 h. Sustained severe-range BP for >15 min = life-threatening emergency.

novedades.texto: SSSAO mnemonic: Support, Safety, magnesium sulfate (loading dose 4-6 g IV, maintenance 1-2 g/h until 24 h postpartum), Antihypertensives (reduce by 20-25% over 24-48 h, target 135/85 per NICE), Obstetric management (fetal maturation at 24-34 weeks, fetal well-being, delivery: non-severe PE at 37 weeks, severe PE at 34 weeks). Stepwise hypertensive emergency algorithm: IV labetalol 20→40 mg / oral nifedipine 10→20→20 mg / IV hydralazine 10 mg, reassessing every 10-20 min. Crisis target (ISH 2026): with BP ≥160/110, hospitalize and lower to SBP <160 and DBP <105 mmHg within 2-3 h, avoiding abrupt drops and always together with magnesium sulfate. Once reached, maintenance aims at <140/90 (ISH 2026) or 135/85 (NICE), avoiding excessively low values. IV alternatives cited by ISH 2026 (Table 15, severe preeclampsia, eclampsia and HELLP): first line labetalol or nicardipine, with magnesium sulfate; it also lists esmolol, hydralazine and urapidil as alternatives. Esmolol and urapidil have little experience in pregnancy and limited availability in Paraguay: they are not part of the CaVeSal® stepwise scheme, but are recorded here for what they are, alternatives cited by the guideline. Fluid management: no bolus, total 80 mL/h or 1 mL/kg/h, max 125 mL/h. Eclampsia: seizure control with a 4-6 g IV MgSO4 bolus (or 2 g IV if already receiving it), maintenance 2 g/h, second 2 g IV bolus if seizures recur. Intubate if: unconscious after seizure, status epilepticus, aspiration, hypoxia. Continue MgSO4 for at least 24 h postpartum or from the last seizure.

Additional severity criterion — Progressive renal insufficiency: serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubling of baseline creatinine (not previously included alongside LDH/bilirubin — added as an independent laboratory criterion). Two administration-rate options: 3-5 min (MSPBS/CaVeSal regimen) or 10 min (ACOG/WHO). novedades.fuentes: WHO Study Group. Assessment of fracture risk and its application to screening for postmenopausal osteoporosis. novedades.texto: Clasificación OMS por T-score, Z-score en premenopausia (ISCD), FRAX, muy alto riesgo y conducta (BHOF y AACE). Algoritmo propio CaVeSal® · Basado en: OMS 1994 · ISCD 2023 · BHOF 2022 · AACE 2020 · Endocrine Society 2019/2020 · USPSTF 2025 Cargá los T-score (acepta negativos con coma) o el Z-score en premenopausia, fracturas y FRAX. Devuelve la clasificación, si hay indicación de tratamiento, el muy alto riesgo y el control. Los valores se copian del informe: la app no lee el PDF ni la foto. Según la ISCD, el diagnóstico lo define el T-score más bajo entre columna, cuello femoral y cadera total, y la app indica en qué región está. Con indicación de tratamiento sugiere alendronato, risedronato o ácido zoledrónico (reducen fracturas vertebrales, no vertebrales y de cadera); el ibandronato solo demostró reducir fracturas vertebrales, así que con riesgo en cadera la conducta indica no usarlo. También clasifica cada región por separado, avisa si entre columna y cadera hay más de 1 desvío de diferencia (posible artrosis o calcificación que eleva la columna) y, en la posmenopausia, con Z-score de −2,0 o menos sugiere buscar una causa secundaria. Guías relacionadas de la Historia Clínica: Osteoporosis y densitometría ósea (DXA); Vitamina K2 (MK-7) — Salud ósea y vascular.

novedades.texto: T-Score: normal ≥-1.0 · osteopenia -1.0 to -2.5 · osteoporosis ≤-2.5 · severe +fracture. Z-Score (premenopausal): ≤-2.0 abnormal. ISCD criterion: the diagnosis is set by the lowest T-score among lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip (not the average). The T-score compares with young adult women (white, 20–29 years, NHANES III); the Z-score, with the same age and sex. FRAX (osteopenia, established postmenopause): treat if major fracture risk ≥20% or hip ≥3%. FRAX and OST are not useful to identify perimenopausal women who will develop osteoporosis. Basic support (all patients): Elemental calcium 1,000-1,500mg/day + Vitamin D3 800-2,000 IU/day (target ≥30ng/mL). Antiresorptives: Alendronate 70mg PO weekly · Risedronate 35mg weekly or 150mg monthly · Zoledronic acid 5mg IV annually · Denosumab 60mg SC every 6 months (do not stop abruptly without transitioning to another antiresorptive, due to rebound vertebral fracture risk). Anabolics (severe osteoporosis/high fracture risk): Teriparatide 20mcg/day SC, maximum 24 months of use. Treatment by risk category (SVGO 2026, Swiss guideline): imminent or very high risk → anabolic first, then antiresorptive consolidation; romosozumab or abaloparatide when the fastest BMD gain is needed, especially at the hip. High risk → bisphosphonates or denosumab first line. Moderate risk → lifestyle + raloxifene or oral bisphosphonate; in selected osteopenia or early osteoporosis, infrequent zoledronate as prevention. Treat-to-target by hip BMD, reassess at 2 years. Check local availability of romosozumab and abaloparatide. Prevention of bone loss in perimenopause and menopause Prevention ≠ treatment: treatment is given to women at high current fracture risk; prevention aims to maintain bone density so that osteoporosis does not develop later. Bone loss is fastest in the year before and the first years after the final menstrual period (≈10% at the spine and ≈9% at the hip at 5 years, almost 1 T-score unit); abrupt estrogen withdrawal (oophorectomy, stopping MHT) accelerates it. Higher risk: the best predictor is bone density on entering perimenopause — with a T-score <−1.0 most women reach osteoporosis (≤−2.5) before age 65. Risk factors for low BMD: weight <57 kg, prolonged amenorrhea after puberty or delayed puberty (Turner syndrome, exercise-related amenorrhea), previous fracture, family history of osteoporosis, illnesses or drugs that harm the skeleton. Densitometry (DXA): in every perimenopausal woman with any of these factors, to identify those with a T-score <−1.0 who benefit most from prevention. Nutrition, supplements and exercise: advisable for all women, but they do not prevent menopause-related bone loss (calcium, vitamin D, vitamin K2, collagen, phytoestrogens and the various exercise regimens at best slow it modestly). Estrogen: oral, transdermal or systemic-dose vaginal MHT prevents bone loss for as long as it is used (also combined with a progestogen or bazedoxifene) and reduces spine and hip fractures by 30–40%. Consider it in women reaching menopause with a T-score <−1.0. Best response in early postmenopause with oral estradiol 2mg or a 0.1mg/day patch; in perimenopause, contraceptives with 20µg ethinyl estradiol are effective. Lower doses protect a smaller proportion of women (the 0.014mg patch was only studied in late postmenopause, ages 60–80). No serum estradiol target has been validated; with transdermal products it can be measured to check absorption. No fixed duration limit; individualize. When estrogen is stopped: the bone benefit is lost within 12 months. Give a bisphosphonate for 2–3 years (alendronate, or one zoledronic acid infusion), then raloxifene or intermittent bisphosphonate to maintain density. If estrogen is contraindicated: approved for prevention are raloxifene (weak effect, does not fully prevent loss) and the bisphosphonates alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate and zoledronate. For prevention, alendronate and zoledronate are used at half the treatment dose: alendronate 35mg PO weekly for 3–5 years, or zoledronic acid 2 doses 2 years apart; then intermittent bisphosphonate. MHT without vasomotor symptoms: The Menopause Society considers it reasonable to prevent bone loss in women at high risk of osteoporosis; the USPSTF (2022) recommends against MHT for the primary prevention of chronic conditions. Use shared decision-making. CaVeSal® own algorithm · Based on: McClung MR, Clark AL. Menopause 2026;33(11):1209-1211 (The Menopause Society) · Bolland MJ, et al. NEJM 2025 · USPSTF 2022. Treatment choice in postmenopause (Endocrine Society 2019/2020, AACE 2020, NOGG 2022, BHOF 2022): Very high risk (recent or multiple fractures, T-score ≤-3.0, fracture on treatment): anabolic first (teriparatide 20 µg/day SC or abaloparatide 80 µg/day SC up to 2 years, or romosozumab 210 mg/month SC for 12 months, not after MI or stroke in the past year), then an antiresorptive. MHT as first line: under 60 years or less than 10 years since menopause, with symptoms and no contraindication; it prevents all fracture types. If stopped, switch to another treatment. Bisphosphonate (first line otherwise): alendronate 70 mg/week or risedronate 35 mg/week PO, or zoledronic acid 5 mg IV yearly. Reassess at 5 years (oral) or 3 years (IV): if low or moderate risk, holiday of up to 5 years; if high risk, continue. Alendronate, risedronate and zoledronic acid reduce vertebral, nonvertebral and hip fractures. Ibandronate (150 mg/month PO): similar spine BMD gain, but only shown to reduce vertebral fractures, not hip or nonvertebral ones; do not use it when the risk is at the hip (Endocrine Society 2019, AACE 2020, BHOF 2022). Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months: initial alternative or if bisphosphonates are not tolerated, contraindicated or fail. Do not delay or stop without switching to another antiresorptive (bisphosphonate, MHT or SERM), due to rebound vertebral fractures. Clearance <35 mL/min: avoid bisphosphonates; denosumab with adequate calcium and vitamin D and serum calcium monitoring. Raloxifene 60 mg/day: high vertebral risk with low VTE risk and high breast cancer risk; not indicated with VTE risk or history; may worsen hot flashes. Calcium 1,000–1,200 mg/day, preferably from diet, and vitamin D 800–1,000 IU/day (BHOF 2022).

Algoritmo propio CaVeSal® · Basado en: Guías CaVeSal® · ACOG PB 193, CO 783 y PB 218 · NICE NG126 · CDC 2021 · RCOG GTG 41 · Roma IV · AUA 2022 Agudo: estabilidad, β-hCG y ecografía; si es positiva, embarazo intrauterino, ectópico (metotrexato o cirugía) o de localización desconocida con β-hCG a las 48 horas; si es negativa, torsión, EPI, absceso, quiste roto, apendicitis y causas urinarias. Crónico: 6 meses o más, banderas rojas, causas probables (endometriosis, adenomiosis, congestión pélvica, adherencias, vejiga dolorosa, colon irritable, miofascial, neuropático, psicosocial), estudios y conducta. Guías relacionadas de la Historia Clínica: Dolor pélvico agudo y crónico — Causas y conducta.

novedades.texto: Día de ovulación, ventana de progesterona y tamaño folicular para el trigger. Algoritmo propio CaVeSal® · Basado en: ASRM 2013 y 2020, ESHRE 2023 y 2025, MSPyBS 2025 1Cargá la duración del ciclo en días: desde el primer día de una menstruación hasta el primer día de la siguiente. 2Si cargás la fecha de la última menstruación, la app muestra también la fecha de ovulación y la del dosaje de progesterona. 3Versión completa Elegí el esquema de inducción (clomifeno, letrozol o gonadotropinas) y el diámetro del folículo líder en milímetros. 4La app indica si el folículo está en rango para el trigger, por debajo o por encima del tamaño recomendado. Rangos del folículo líder Clomifeno: 20 a 28 mm, con mejores tasas entre 23 y 28 mm. Letrozol: 19 a 23 mm, tolerado hasta 28 mm. Gonadotropinas: 16 a 18 mm, tolerado hasta 20 mm. Fertilidad en Demo: ovulación y progesteronaVersión completa: esquema y folículo líder En la Demo, el esquema y el folículo quedan ocultos y aparece el aviso de la versión completa. Algoritmo propio CaVeSal® · Basado en: US MEC 2024 (con apéndices E, F, I y J) · OMS 2025 y 2026 · FSRH 2023 · prospectos FDA de Mounjaro (08/2026) y Ozempic (05/2026) · OMS 2018 · Trussell 2011 Un solo módulo en 3 pasos. Arriba, el bloque de categorías de la OMS 1 a 4 y el botón (i) Leyenda con las tres lecturas, I/C, A/C/D y A/C/D/S. Paso 1: edad, método actual e iniciación o continuación. Paso 2: tocá cada condición o su variante; el buscador las filtra y arriba quedan las marcadas, con × para quitarlas. Incluye barrera, naturales, emergencia e incretinas. Paso 3: la Sugerencia CaVeSal® y los métodos por familia (DIU, solo progestágeno, combinados, lactancia, barrera, emergencia, esterilización y naturales), con filtros. Tocá un método para ver su ficha: Pearl, duración, composición, por qué tiene esa categoría y, en los combinados, las formas de uso (secuencial, extendido fijo, flexible y continuo). novedades.texto: Espermograma OMS 2021 con diagnóstico, REM, ovulación y su causa, reserva ovárica, útero y trompas, y el siguiente paso según los resultados. Algoritmo propio CaVeSal® · Basado en: OMS 2025 · OMS 2021 · ASRM 2026 · AUA/ASRM 2024 · ESHRE 2023 · ASRM 2020 y 2021 · RCPI 2023 Cuándo estudiar: con la edad y los meses buscando, indica si corresponde iniciar el estudio (12 meses, 6 con 35 años o más, inmediato con 40 o más o con causa conocida). Ambos miembros se estudian a la vez. Factor masculino: cargá el espermograma; se compara con los límites de la OMS 2021 y se nombra el hallazgo (oligo, asteno, terato, azoospermia). Si es anormal, se repite tras 11 semanas o más y se deriva a urología. El REM tras capacitación orienta IIU, FIV o ICSI con la escala de la guía HC (Sugerencia CaVeSal®). Factor ovulatorio, reserva y útero-trompas: ciclos, progesterona lútea, FSH, prolactina, TSH y signos de SOMP orientan la causa de anovulación. RFA y AMH clasifican la reserva (no son prueba de fertilidad). Elegí la prueba tubaria (HSG, HyCoSy/HyFoSy, laparoscopia) y su resultado. Siguiente paso: resume la conducta prioritaria de la pareja, los estudios que faltan y si conviene IIU o FIV según el pronóstico. Guías relacionadas de la Historia Clínica: Algoritmo de estudio de la pareja infértil — Siguiente paso según resultados; Espermiograma y REM (factor masculino); Algoritmo de estudio — Factor femenino; Permeabilidad tubárica — HyFoSy, HSG e histeroscopia; Enfoque OMS 2025 para el estudio de infertilidad.

novedades.texto: Semáforo de riesgo del MSPBS, dosis y momento del ácido fólico, TSH con anti-TPO y anti-Tg, valores del día 2 y del día 21, y alertas de lupus, SAF y trombofilia. Tabla adaptada del MSPBS 2022, p. 23 · OMS · ACOG/SMFM 2022 · USPSTF 2023 · CDC · Algoritmo propio CaVeSal® · Basado en: ASRM 2020 · ATA 2017 Semáforo: cargá edad, peso, talla, hemoglobina, palidez, sífilis y VIH, y marcá los criterios rojos y amarillos que tenga. Gana el color más alto. Si falta un dato obligatorio, no se clasifica en verde. Cada color muestra la conducta del MSPBS, y las ambigüedades del cuadro (35 años, Hb entre 11 y 12, IMC de 30) aparecen explicadas. Ácido fólico: dosis según el color y las indicaciones de dosis alta (defecto del tubo neural previo, diabetes, epilepsia, IMC de 30 o más), con el momento de inicio y fin. Si marcás variante de MTHFR, muestra que no cambia la dosis ni el tipo. Panel hormonal: todos los valores son opcionales. FSH, LH, AMH, TSH y prolactina se dosan del día 2 al 5 del ciclo; la progesterona, el día 21. La TSH se interpreta con el anti-TPO, la levotiroxina, la FIV/ICSI y el límite superior del laboratorio (4,0 si no lo informa). Anti-Tg, autoinmunidad y trombofilia: el anti-Tg suma información de autoinmunidad tiroidea; la decisión de levotiroxina sigue basada en el anti-TPO. Si marcás lupus, SAF obstétrico o trombótico, anticuerpos antifosfolípidos, trombosis previa o trombofilia, se muestran las alertas preconcepcionales (ACR 2020, SMFM #64, ACOG PB 197) con enlace a la guía. En el algoritmo combinado, además de las contraindicaciones clásicas, marcá los antecedentes oncológicos: cada uno muestra si la THM sistémica no se recomienda, si se decide con oncología o si no la contraindica, según la histología y el estadio. Con Prevención de osteoporosis y riesgo de fractura alto o muy alto, aparece el tratamiento: THM de primera línea en menores de 60 años o con menos de 10 años de menopausia y síntomas, bifosfonato con su pausa, denosumab (sin suspender sin pasar a otro antirresortivo), raloxifeno, anabólico en riesgo muy alto y calcio con vitamina D. El T-score y el riesgo de Densitometría se cargan solos. novedades.titulo: Combined contraception: regimens, patch and rings
novedades.fuentes: FSRH. Combined Hormonal Contraception, 2023 · OMS. Nota de prensa 23-09-2026 · FDA. Annovera (segesterone acetate/ethinyl estradiol) label, 2018 · ISP Chile, monografía Progering F-25553-20
novedades.texto: Combined regimens per FSRH 2023: standard 21/7, shortened 24/4, extended fixed, flexible and continuous, monophasic only. WHO 2026: extended up to 6 months or continuous up to 1 year. Standard: 21 active days and 7-day break. Extended fixed: 3 packs back to back (63 days) and 4–7-day break. Flexible: continuous use until 3–4 days of bleeding, then a 4-day break (minimum 21 days in a row). Continuous: no break. The break must never exceed 7 days. Benefits of extended or continuous use: fewer bleeds, fewer hormone-free interval symptoms and lower risk of ovulation after missed pills. Combined patch and ring allow the same regimens. Annual ring (Annovera, FDA 2018): segesterone 0.15 mg/day + ethinyl estradiol 0.013 mg/day, 21 days in and 7 out, 13 cycles with the same ring; Pearl 2.98; not studied with BMI >29. Progesterone ring (Progering): only for breastfeeding women (see breastfeeding guide). Nestorone transdermal spray: investigational. Calculated in CaVeSal® GYN, Contraception: eligibility and methods module.

novedades.fuentes: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Tirzepatide prescribing information (ZEPBOUND/MOUNJARO) · Imbroane M, LeMoine K, Nau C, et al. AJOG 2025;233(2):116.e1-e7 (preconception cohort, n=8,534) · FDA. Mounjaro prescribing information, rev. 08/2026 · FDA. Ozempic prescribing information, rev. 05/2026
novedades.texto: Tirzepatide's dual GIP/GLP-1 agonism slows gastric emptying more markedly than pure GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide) — this can reduce the absorption of oral drugs, including oral hormonal contraceptives. Recommendation: use a non-oral contraceptive method, or add a barrier method, for 4 weeks after starting tirzepatide and after each dose escalation — not only once at treatment start. ⚠️ Do not confuse with preconception washout (next guide): this 4-week window is due to a pharmacokinetic interaction with the oral contraceptive, while preconception washout is the recommended time to stop the drug before trying to conceive — two distinct concepts, with different durations, and both may apply to the same patient at different times. Practical approach for a patient on tirzepatide who is losing weight and recovering fertility, and who is not seeking pregnancy: prefer non-oral methods whenever possible — LARC (subdermal implant, IUD/IUS — see LARC guide), injectable (DMPA), patch, or vaginal ring — since these do not depend on gastrointestinal absorption and sidestep the underlying problem; if the patient already uses or prefers an oral contraceptive, add a barrier method (condom) for the 4 weeks after starting and after each dose escalation, without needing to stop the oral agent. Discuss contraception from the start of GLP-1/GIP treatment in every woman of reproductive age, not only when she presents seeking pregnancy (see the GLP-1 and fertility recovery guide). Imbroane et al. (AJOG 2025, observational preconception cohort of 8,534 women) document the underlying clinical context — women recovering ovulatory cycles and fertility during GLP-1/GIP use — that supports the need for this proactive contraceptive conversation, although the study does not directly evaluate contraceptive failure rates. FDA Mounjaro label data (revised 08/2026): after a single 5 mg dose, ethinyl estradiol Cmax fell 59% and norgestimate 66%, with AUC ~20% lower and delayed absorption; with acetaminophen, Cmax fell 50% after the first dose with no relevant effect at week 4. Semaglutide (FDA Ozempic label, 05/2026): no clinically relevant interaction with ethinyl estradiol/levonorgestrel; with severe vomiting or diarrhea, add barrier as with any oral method. CaVeSal® suggestion: calculated in the Contraception: eligibility and methods module of CaVeSal® GYN.

novedades.texto: LAM (>98%): amenorrhea + exclusive breastfeeding + <6 months postpartum, all three together. Progestin-only: Cat 1-2 from the start. Combined: Cat 4 if <6 wk breastfeeding; improves over time. Copper IUD: Cat 1 immediate (<48h) or delayed (≥4wk); Cat 3 in between. Progesterone vaginal ring (Progering): natural progesterone 10 mg/day, 90 days per ring, up to 4 consecutive rings; inserted at 4–9 weeks postpartum and requires breastfeeding at least 4 times a day; efficacy comparable to the copper IUD while breastfeeding continues (Sivin 1997; Massai 1999); registered in Chile (ISP) and other Latin American countries; no category in US MEC 2024. Nestorone transdermal spray: investigational, not approved.

novedades.titulo: Hereditary cancer — BRCA and Lynch syndrome
novedades.fuentes: NCCN Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment: Breast, Ovarian, Pancreatic and Prostate · NCCN Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment: Colorectal, Endometrial and Gastric · ACOG PB 182 · ACOG PB 147 · Amsterdam II criteria (1999) · MSPBS Paraguay, Gynecological Pathologies Manual 2025
novedades.texto: Refer for genetic counseling (breast and ovary): known familial pathogenic variant (cascade testing) · breast cancer at 45 or younger (MSPBS 2025) or 50 or younger (NCCN) · triple negative (NCCN any age; MSPBS up to 60) · bilateral or multiple primaries · breast cancer with a close relative with breast cancer at 50 or younger, ovarian, pancreatic or metastatic prostate cancer · Ashkenazi ancestry · epithelial ovarian, tubal or peritoneal cancer at any age · exocrine pancreatic · metastatic prostate · male breast cancer in the family · 3 or more relatives on the same side with breast cancer. First-degree relative with breast cancer at 50 or younger: risk model (Tyrer-Cuzick, CanRisk) and test if variant probability is above 5 %. Lynch syndrome: every endometrial and colorectal cancer with MMR immunohistochemistry or MSI on the tumor (universal screening). Refer with dMMR or MSI tumor (except MLH1 loss due to promoter hypermethylation, probably sporadic), endometrial or colorectal cancer before 50, Amsterdam II criteria (3 or more relatives, 2 generations, one before 50), 3 or more relatives with spectrum cancers even without full Amsterdam, or PREMM5 ≥2.5 %. Testing: multigene panel with informed consent (BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, RAD51C, RAD51D, BRIP1, TP53, PTEN, CDH1, STK11, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 and EPCAM). A negative result without a known familial variant does not rule out risk; a VUS does not change management. BRCA1/2 carriers: breast: clinical exam every 6–12 months and annual MRI from 25, annual mammography from 30; discuss risk-reducing mastectomy. Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy at 35–40 (BRCA1) or 40–45 (BRCA2) after childbearing. Ultrasound and CA-125 are not effective screening. COCs reduce ovarian cancer risk. After oophorectomy before natural menopause, MHT until the age of menopause if no breast cancer. Others: PALB2: annual MRI and mammography from 30; consider salpingo-oophorectomy from 45. RAD51C, RAD51D or BRIP1: salpingo-oophorectomy at 45–50. Lynch: MLH1, MSH2 or EPCAM: colonoscopy every 1–2 years from 20–25. MSH6 and PMS2: every 1–3 years from 30–35. Risk-reducing hysterectomy with salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing, usually around 40 (PMS2: hysterectomy optional; ovarian risk not clearly increased). Endometrial biopsy every 1–2 years from 30–35, optional until surgery. Cascade testing of first-degree relatives; individualized aspirin.

novedades.titulo: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) for contraception
novedades.fuentes: CDC US MEC 2024 · WHO MEC 6th ed. (2025) · SIC 2025 · FSRH (2017, amended 2023) · CDC. US MEC 2024, MMWR Recomm Rep 2024;73(4), apéndices E, F, I, J · FDA. Mounjaro (tirzepatide) prescribing information, rev. 08/2026 · FDA. Ozempic (semaglutide) prescribing information, rev. 05/2026 · FSRH. Combined Hormonal Contraception, 2023 · OMS. Nota de prensa 23-09-2026
novedades.texto: Categories: 1 no restriction · 2 advantages generally outweigh risks · 3 risks generally outweigh advantages (only if no other method is available or acceptable, with follow-up) · 4 unacceptable risk, do not use. With several conditions, the highest category applies. Some conditions have one category for initiation and another for continuation. Cat 4 for combined methods (US MEC 2024): breastfeeding or postpartum under 21 days; smoker aged 35 or older with 15 or more cigarettes per day; BP 160/100 or higher or vascular disease; prior VTE with high recurrence risk (no anticoagulation or prophylactic dose); known thrombophilia; major surgery with prolonged immobilization; ischemic heart disease; stroke; complicated valvular disease; peripartum cardiomyopathy (under 6 months or moderately or severely impaired function); SLE with antiphospholipid antibodies; migraine with aura; current breast cancer; decompensated cirrhosis; hepatocellular adenoma or carcinoma; chronic kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome or dialysis); sickle cell disease; transplant with graft failure. Cat 3 to 4 by severity: multiple cardiovascular risk factors, diabetes with end-organ damage or over 20 years' duration. Progestin-only: cat 4 with current breast cancer; cat 3 with past cancer and no disease for 5 years. The 3-monthly injectable (DMPA) is cat 3 with BP 160/100 or higher, vascular disease, ischemic heart disease, stroke, high-risk VTE, thrombophilia and diabetes with end-organ damage. IUD (copper and LNG), cat 4 for initiation: pregnancy, puerperal sepsis, immediately after septic abortion, current PID or purulent cervicitis, chlamydia or gonorrhea, distorted uterine cavity, unexplained bleeding before evaluation, cervical or endometrial cancer awaiting treatment, trophoblastic disease with intrauterine disease, pelvic tuberculosis. Differences with WHO 2025 (6th ed.): progestin injectables while breastfeeding under 6 weeks moved from cat 3 to 2 and can be offered immediately after delivery; nevirapine and ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitors moved to cat 1 with all hormonal methods (US MEC 2024 keeps cat 2 or 3 for some); with PrEP all methods are cat 1; repeated emergency contraception in the same cycle is cat 1; inflammatory bowel disease was added. Over 40 (SIC consensus 2025): cardiovascular safety is the main factor. Estrogen-free methods do not increase venous or arterial risk. Among combined methods, EE/levonorgestrel, EE/norgestimate and natural estradiol increase VTE the least; EE 20 µg with drospirenone and natural estradiol do not increase arterial risk. Heavy bleeding, from most to least effective: LNG-IUD 52 mg, estradiol valerate/dienogest, ring, COC with EE 30-35 µg, progestin-only. COCs protect bone; the implant, progestin-only pill and LNG-IUD are neutral. When to stop contraception (FSRH): generally at 55. Non-hormonal method: 2 years of amenorrhea under 50 and 1 year at 50 or older. Combined and DMPA: until 50, then switch method. Implant, progestin-only pill or LNG-IUD with amenorrhea from age 50: if FSH is above 30 IU/L, stop after 1 more year. FSH is not useful on combined methods or MHT. MHT can be added to a non-combined method. Other data: tirzepatide may reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives; use a non-oral method or add a barrier for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase (FDA label). The etonogestrel implant is approved for 5 years (ANMAT 2025). 2026 update (calculated in CaVeSal® GYN, Contraception: eligibility and methods module). Barrier (US MEC 2024, appendix E): almost all category 1; diaphragm 2 with recurrent UTI, complicated valvular disease or prior births; spermicide and diaphragm 4 with high HIV risk and 3 with HIV; diaphragm 3 with history of toxic shock; latex condom and diaphragm 3 with latex allergy. Fertility awareness-based methods (appendix F; A accept, C caution, D delay; symptoms / calendar): breastfeeding <6 weeks D/D and ≥6 weeks C/D; postpartum not breastfeeding <4 weeks D/D; post-abortion C/D; irregular bleeding D/D; vaginal discharge D/A; cycle-altering drugs C or D; acute fever D/A; post-menarche and perimenopause C/C. Emergency (appendix J; copper IUD / ulipristal / levonorgestrel / Yuzpe): pregnancy 4/NA/NA/NA; obesity 1/2/2/2; history of severe cardiovascular disease 1/2/2/2; migraine 1/1/1/2; severe liver disease 1/2/2/2; CYP3A4 inducers 1/2/2/2; RA on immunosuppression, transplant with graft failure and sexual assault 2/1/1/1; breastfeeding, prior ectopic, bariatric surgery, IBD and repeated use 1. Sterilization: US MEC assigns no categories; WHO uses A/C/D/S (S: special setting, with experienced team and equipment). Tirzepatide (FDA Mounjaro label, revised 08/2026): after a single 5 mg dose, ethinyl estradiol Cmax fell 59% and norgestimate 66%, with AUC ~20% lower; it advises a non-oral method or adding barrier for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase; non-oral hormonal methods are not affected. Semaglutide (FDA Ozempic label, 05/2026): no clinically relevant interaction with ethinyl estradiol/levonorgestrel; caution with vomiting. Combined regimens (FSRH 2023): standard 21/7, extended fixed, flexible and continuous, monophasic only. WHO (23-09-2026): combined methods in extended use up to 6 months or continuous up to 1 year, implant up to 5 years, and mifepristone as emergency contraception.

novedades.fuentes: ADA, Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49 Suppl 1), section 2 · WHO 2006 and 2011
novedades.texto: Diabetes: fasting ≥126 mg/dL · 2-h OGTT ≥200 · HbA1c ≥6.5 % · random glucose ≥200 with classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) or hyperglycemic crisis. Prediabetes (ADA): fasting 100–125 · 2-h OGTT 140–199 · HbA1c 5.7–6.4 %. WHO sets impaired fasting glucose from 110. Confirmation: two tests in the diabetes range (same or different samples) confirm. A single value: repeat the same or another test on a second sample. Random ≥200 with symptoms needs no second test; without symptoms it does not diagnose alone. Diabetes: follow-up by internal medicine or diabetology and screening for complications (fundus, renal function and albuminuria, foot, lipids, blood pressure). Effective contraception until good control (check MEC). If planning pregnancy: HbA1c below 6.5 % if achievable without hypoglycemia and folic acid before conception. Prediabetes: lifestyle (diet, physical activity and 7 % weight loss if overweight), annual glucose testing and consider metformin, especially with BMI ≥35 aged 25 to 59 or history of gestational diabetes. Normal: repeat screening every 3 years, or earlier with risk factors. History of gestational diabetes: screening at least every 3 years for life. Pregnancy: these cut-offs do not apply; IADPSG criteria are used (see gestational diabetes guides).

novedades.titulo: Acute and chronic pelvic pain — Causes and management
novedades.fuentes: ACOG PB 193 (2018) · ACOG CO 783 (2019) · NICE NG126 · CDC 2021 · ACOG PB 218 (2020) · RCOG GTG 41 · Roma IV · AUA IC/BPS 2022 · ESHRE 2022
novedades.texto: Acute, first step: β-hCG in every woman of reproductive age. Hemodynamic instability: resuscitation, blood type, and emergency surgery if hemoperitoneum. Positive β-hCG: intrauterine pregnancy → assess miscarriage or non-obstetric cause (corpus luteum cyst, torsion, appendicitis); after fertility treatment, consider heterotopic pregnancy. Empty uterus with β-hCG ≥3,500 mIU/mL (discriminatory zone): high suspicion of ectopic or non-viable pregnancy. Below the discriminatory zone: repeat β-hCG at 48 h; rise ≥35 % compatible with viable pregnancy, fall ≥50 % resolving pregnancy, intermediate change suspicious for ectopic. Ectopic: unstable or hemoperitoneum → laparoscopic salpingectomy or laparotomy. Methotrexate 50 mg/m² IM single dose if stable, unruptured, β-hCG ≤5,000, no embryonic cardiac activity and reliable follow-up; β-hCG on days 4 and 7 (must fall ≥15 %), then weekly until negative. Contraindicated with coexisting intrauterine pregnancy, breastfeeding, immunodeficiency, hepatic, renal or pulmonary disease, blood dyscrasia or active ulcer. Expectant only with low and falling β-hCG (e.g. <1,500). Rh negative: anti-D. Negative β-hCG: adnexal torsion (sudden pain, vomiting, mass) → urgent laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian conservation; normal Doppler does not exclude it · PID (cervical motion tenderness, fever, discharge) and tubo-ovarian abscess (admission, parenteral antibiotics, drainage if no response or 7–8 cm or more) · hemorrhagic or ruptured cyst (stable: expectant with analgesia and hemoglobin control) · ovulation pain · appendicitis · urinary cause · fibroid degeneration · malpositioned IUD. Chronic, red flags: postmenopausal or postcoital bleeding, weight loss, pelvic mass, rectal bleeding or change in bowel habit after 50, hematuria or onset after 50 → investigate malignancy before attributing pain to a functional cause. Chronic causes and management: endometriosis (empirical treatment without laparoscopy: NSAID with continuous contraceptive, dienogest 2 mg/day or LNG-IUD) · adenomyosis (LNG-IUD, dienogest) · pelvic congestion (Doppler; progestogens; selected embolization) · adhesions (adhesiolysis only if dense and related to pain) · bladder pain syndrome · irritable bowel syndrome (Rome IV) · myofascial pain (Carnett sign, trigger points: pelvic floor physiotherapy) · neuropathic (gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline) · psychosocial component (depression and violence screening). General: pain map and diary, examination with pelvic floor palpation, transvaginal ultrasound (MRI if unclear); NSAIDs first line and multidisciplinary approach. Diagnostic laparoscopy if empirical treatments fail, not as a first step.

novedades.titulo: Choice of progestogen in MHT and contraception
novedades.fuentes: BMS 2026 · EMA 2013 and 2014 · ESTHER/E3N · Schindler 2008 · Regidor 2018 · LIBERATE · LIFT
novedades.texto: MHT, no uterus: estrogen alone, no progestogen (exception: previous endometriosis, consider a combined regimen). MHT, with uterus: first choice micronized progesterone or dydrogesterone, for lower VTE risk and neutral metabolic profile. VTE risk: micronized progesterone or dydrogesterone with transdermal estradiol; avoid 19-norprogesterone derivatives and oral estrogen (previous VTE contraindicates MHT). Hypertension or fluid retention: drospirenone or micronized progesterone. Bleeding or fibroids: LNG-IUD 52 mg for endometrial protection. Insomnia: micronized progesterone at night. Breast risk: micronized progesterone and dydrogesterone may carry lower risk (observational data). Tibolone: an option with low libido due to its androgenic effect; contraindicated with breast cancer (LIBERATE) and not after 60, as stroke risk outweighs benefit (LIFT). Low libido: avoid strong antiandrogens (cyproterone). Regimen: cyclic in perimenopause or with less than 12 months without menses; continuous after more than 12 months of amenorrhea. Oral contraception: first choice levonorgestrel, norethisterone or norgestimate, for lower VTE risk (EMA). VTE risk: no estrogen (progestogen-only pill, implant or IUD). Acne, hirsutism or PCOS: drospirenone, dienogest or chlormadinone; cyproterone only in moderate to severe acne or hirsutism after failure of topical or antibiotic treatment (VTE 1.5 to 2 times that of LNG). Fluid retention or mastalgia: drospirenone. Endometriosis: dienogest. Heavy bleeding or fibroids: LNG-IUD 52 mg. Hypertension and breast risk: check the MEC category. Meningioma: avoid nomegestrol, chlormadinone and high-dose cyproterone (EMA).

novedades.fuentes: Viroga S. Un nuevo estrógeno: estetrol. Boletín Farmacológico 2025;16(2):1-3 · Creinin MD, et al. Contraception 2021;104(3):222-228 · Gemzell-Danielsson K, et al. BJOG 2022;129(1):63-71 · Douxfils J, et al. Contraception 2020;102:396-402 · AEMPS label, cima.aemps.es, code 1211547001 · Jensen JT, et al. Contraception 2022;116 (análisis combinado fase 3)
novedades.texto: What it is: a natural estrogen of fetal origin (synthesized by the fetal liver from estriol), with tissue-selective activity — agonist in the CNS, bone and genital tissue, antagonist in breast tissue, and little estrogenic effect in liver and vascular tissue. Hepatic metabolism by glucuronidation only (no CYP450 pathway), which reduces the risk of drug interactions. Combined formulation: Estetrol 15mg + Drospirenone 3mg, 1 tablet/day. Efficacy: Pearl Index 1.52 (95% CI 1.04-2.16) in the pivotal phase 3 trials (31 pregnancies / 2,837 women / 26,455 cycles). Regular cycles in 82-94%; spotting ~15% at cycle 12; amenorrhea ~10%. Coagulation/VTE profile: ⚠️ the available literature does not provide a relative risk or odds ratio for VTE versus other combined hormonal contraceptives — this figure is pending verification against the primary articles before being cited as a number. What is documented: a smaller rise in sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG +54% vs. +74% with ethinylestradiol) and smaller changes in lipid profile, with no change in thrombin generation (Douxfils 2020) — surrogate markers suggesting a smaller hepatic/procoagulant impact than ethinylestradiol, but which do not equate to a confirmed clinical VTE risk figure: the pivotal studies recorded 1 case of DVT in 30,289 cycles, too small a number to estimate a comparative rate. The authors themselves note that these advantages remain mostly theoretical and require post-marketing surveillance. Why it may be worth raising in consultation: it is an additional option within the combined contraceptive group, useful for an informed conversation with patients who ask about it specifically — the evidence does not yet support positioning it ahead of established combined methods in terms of thrombotic safety. Pearl Index by trial: 0.47 (CI 0.15–1.11) in Europe/Russia (Gemzell-Danielsson 2022) and 2.65 (CI 1.73–3.88) in USA/Canada (Creinin 2021); 1.52 is the pooled analysis of both (Jensen 2022). 24/4 regimen. Evolution of estrogens in combined pills: ethinyl estradiol (synthetic, greater hepatic effect) → estradiol valerate and 17β-estradiol (identical to natural) → estetrol (natural, fetal origin, tissue-selective). Eligibility: US MEC 2024 classifies it like any combined method.

novedades.titulo: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) — Risk, severity and management
novedades.fuentes: RCOG Green-top Guideline 5 (2016) · ASRM 2024 (prevención del SHO moderado and severo)
novedades.texto: Risk factors (ASRM 2024): AMH above 3.4 ng/mL · antral follicle count above 24 · PCOS · previous OHSS · more than 17 follicles larger than 10 mm · estradiol above 3,500 pg/mL · more than 15 oocytes retrieved. Prevention: in ovulation induction, with more than 17 follicles larger than 10 mm or estradiol above 3,500 pg/mL, withhold hCG and cancel the cycle. In IVF: GnRH antagonist protocol, agonist trigger, freeze-all and cabergoline from the trigger day; metformin in PCOS. Severity (RCOG): mild: abdominal bloating or pain · moderate: nausea or vomiting, ultrasound ascites or ovary 8–12 cm · severe: clinical ascites, hydrothorax, oliguria, hematocrit above 45 %, sodium below 135, potassium above 5, albumin below 3.5 g/dL or ovary larger than 12 cm · critical: tense ascites or large hydrothorax, anuria, thromboembolism, ARDS, hematocrit above 55 % or white cells above 25,000. Mild and moderate: outpatient care with review every 2–3 days; daily weight and abdominal girth, drink to thirst, paracetamol (avoid NSAIDs), no penetrative intercourse; laboratory tests and ultrasound; thromboprophylaxis according to risk factors. Severe and critical: admission (critical in intensive care), strict fluid balance, hourly urine output, crystalloids and albumin if hypovolemia or hemoconcentration; prophylactic LMWH until discharge and, if pregnant, until the end of the first trimester; ultrasound-guided paracentesis for tense ascites, persistent oliguria or respiratory compromise; daily laboratory tests; no diuretics with hypovolemia. Also: with pregnancy, late OHSS lasts longer and worsens with rising hCG. Rule out adnexal torsion if pain is sudden and unilateral. Warning signs for the patient: increasing pain or bloating, shortness of breath, scant urine, weight gain of 1 kg or more per day, vomiting preventing drinking, leg pain or swelling, dizziness.

novedades.titulo: MHT after gynecologic cancer and other conditions
novedades.fuentes: BGCS/BMS 2024 (Post Reprod Health 2024) · The Menopause Society (NAMS) 2022 · EMA 2020 and 2022 (meningioma) · BMS 2026 (endometriosis) · USPSTF 2022 (WHI)
novedades.texto: Decision by histology and stage, always together with oncology. In all cases offer non-hormonal options first or in parallel. Does not contraindicate MHT: high-grade epithelial, mucinous, clear cell or germ cell ovarian cancer (not hormone-dependent; start after treatment ends, not alongside biologic therapies) · squamous cervical, vulvar or vaginal cancer (if irradiated with uterus in place, add a progestogen) · BRCA or Lynch with risk-reducing surgery and no cancer (MHT advised until age 51; with uterus, add a progestogen). Decide with oncology: stage I–II, grade 1–2 endometrioid endometrial cancer (studies show no higher recurrence) · stage I low-grade serous ovarian cancer · serous borderline or endometrioid ovarian tumor (caution and shared decision) · cervical adenocarcinoma (may express estrogen receptors; after radical hysterectomy, estrogen alone; after chemoradiation with uterus, continuous combined). Systemic MHT not recommended: stage III–IV, grade 3 or non-endometrioid endometrial cancer · low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma or other uterine sarcoma (low-grade ESS also contraindicates vaginal estrogen) · stage II–IV or recurrent low-grade serous ovarian cancer and granulosa cell tumor. Vaginal therapy is decided with oncology. Current or past meningioma: avoid nomegestrol and chlormadinone (contraindicated) and high-dose cyproterone (EMA 2020 and 2022). Other conditions: established coronary disease: do not start systemic MHT · gallstones or gallbladder disease: oral MHT increases it (WHI), use the transdermal route · endometriosis, even without a uterus: continuous combined therapy instead of estrogen alone, at least until age 51 · prior endometrial hyperplasia: continuous progestogen at adequate dose and investigate any bleeding · MHT is not indicated to prevent dementia or cardiovascular disease (NAMS 2022).

Transvaginal cervical ultrasound (TVUS): Cervical length (CL) >30mm → high negative predictive value (rules out active preterm labor). CL <25mm (or <20mm) → short cervix / elevated risk. Biomarkers if CL 20-30mm: fetal fibronectin (fFN) or PAMG-1 (PartoSure) — if negative, avoids unnecessary tocolysis.

novedades.fuentes: Tabla propia CaVeSal® · Based on: ACOG PB 217 (2020) · FASGO consensus (2018; 2022 update) · Rev Colomb Obstet Ginecol 2015;66(4) · ACOG/SMFM OCC No. 6 (2017). · CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Alao AI et al. Arch Gynecol Obstet 2023;307(2):447-452.
novedades.texto: Definitions by society: ACOG PB 217 / NICE / FIGO: rupture of membranes before the onset of labor; preterm (PPROM) if before 37 0/7 wk. FASGO consensus: at least 2 h before the onset of labor. Colombian guideline (2015): more than 1 h before the onset of labor. Latency: time from rupture to the onset of labor. Prolonged PROM: more than 24 h. Epidemiology: PPROM in 2-3% of pregnancies and term PROM in 8% (ACOG PB 217). Periviability: 20 0/7-25 6/7 wk. Survival to discharge: 23 wk 23-27%, 24 wk 42-59%, 25 wk 67-76% (ACOG/SMFM OCC No. 6, 2017; data from the USA, England and Australia before 2017). Tabla propia CaVeSal® · Based on: ACOG PB 217 (2020) · FASGO consensus (2018; 2022 update) · Rev Colomb Obstet Ginecol 2015;66(4) · ACOG/SMFM OCC No. 6 (2017). Clinical: clear fluid leaking from the vagina — reliability >90% if visualized at the external cervical os on speculum examination. Confirmatory tests: Fern test. Nitrazine test (pH>6.5 turns blue). Biomarkers: PAMG-1 (AmniSure) is the reference non-invasive test in equivocal cases, owing to its higher specificity; IGFBP-1 + AFP (AmnioQuick Duo+) has comparable accuracy; IGFBP-1 (Actim PROM). Interpret together with the clinical assessment. Measurement of urea and creatinine in vaginal secretions — urea 94%/82% and creatinine 98%/90% (sensitivity/specificity, Alao 2023); low cost, useful in resource-limited settings. See comparative table in subcard 7. Adjunct test: cutoffs not standardized; not adopted by ACOG, RCOG, NICE or FIGO guidelines. Amniocentesis: now reserved for selected cases because it is invasive. Uses: (1) definitive diagnosis of PROM with indigo carmine or fluorescein (vaginal tampon, check staining at 20-60 min); (2) subclinical intra-amniotic infection (20-34 wk): glucose, Gram stain, aerobic/anaerobic and mycoplasma cultures; (3) lung maturity — non-invasive alternative: quantusFLM (ultrasound texture analysis of the fetal lung; sensitivity 74-86%, specificity 87-89%; data in PROM are more limited), useful when the timing of delivery is uncertain. Methylene blue: used in the past; now contraindicated (see below). Methylene blue CONTRAINDICATED for intra-amniotic use — teratogenic; causes neonatal jejunal/ileal atresia, severe hyperbilirubinemia, fetal methemoglobinemia, and hemolysis. Safe alternatives: indigo carmine or fluorescein. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Alao AI et al. Arch Gynecol Obstet 2023;307(2):447-452. Microbiological analysis of amniotic fluid: Gram stain, culture (aerobes/anaerobes/Mycoplasma/Ureaplasma), amniotic fluid glucose (<14 mg/dL suggests intra-amniotic infection), leukocyte count.

Antibiotics may be considered from 20 wk; corticosteroids and MgSO4 only if resuscitation is planned (SMFM #71). 24⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷ wk Inpatient expectant management; corticosteroids, latency antibiotics, magnesium sulfate if <32 wk and delivery is imminent. 34⁰/⁷-36⁶/⁷ wk Expectant management or delivery (ACOG PB 217; PPROMT); expectant management until 37 wk only in the absence of infection and with close monitoring. ≥37 wk Induction within 12-24 h. Cervical elastography and amniotic sludge as emerging risk markers. Not an acute management protocol. AI does not replace clinical judgment; it enhances its analytical capacity to support better decision-making (FLASOG 2026).

novedades.fuentes: CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG PB 217 (2020) · FIGO · SMFM Consult Series #71 (2024) · ACOG Practice Advisory (2025) · PPROMT, Morris et al. Lancet 2016.
novedades.texto: Gestational age Management Previable (<22-24 wk) Expectant management as an outpatient/inpatient; counseling on the risk of pulmonary hypoplasia, deformities, and stillbirth. Offer pregnancy termination or expectant management to all (SMFM #71, GRADE 1C). No tocolysis. Latency antibiotics may be considered from 20⁰/⁷ to 23⁶/⁷ (2C) and are recommended from 24⁰/⁷ (1B). Corticosteroids and MgSO4 only once neonatal resuscitation is planned (1B). Inform of the higher maternal risk with expectant management: morbidity 60.2% vs 33% and severe morbidity 12% vs 5% (ACOG 2025). Preterm, remote from term (24⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷ wk) Expectant inpatient management; complete course of antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone/dexamethasone); magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if delivery is imminent and GA<32 wk; mandatory latency antibiotic prophylaxis; tocolysis contraindicated or limited to 48h to complete corticosteroid treatment (if no infection). Late preterm (34⁰/⁷-36⁶/⁷ wk) ACOG PB 217: expectant management or proceed to delivery (induction or cesarean as indicated). PPROMT (Lancet 2016): no difference in neonatal sepsis (2% vs 3%); immediate delivery had more respiratory distress (8% vs 5%) and more cesareans (26% vs 19%); expectant management had more hemorrhage and intrapartum fever. Expectant management until 37 weeks only if there are no signs of infection + close monitoring. At term (≥37⁰/⁷ wk) Induction (oxytocin or misoprostol if the cervix is unfavorable) within 12-24h to reduce the risk of intrauterine infection. CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG PB 217 (2020) · FIGO · SMFM Consult Series #71 (2024) · ACOG Practice Advisory (2025) · PPROMT, Morris et al. Lancet 2016.

novedades.texto: Contraindicate expectant management at any gestational age: Clinical chorioamnionitis / confirmed intra-amniotic infection (Gibbs criteria). Placental abruption. Acute fetal compromise (non-reassuring FHR / abnormal biophysical profile). Established labor. Fetal death.

novedades.titulo: Fetal lung maturation and neuroprotection (submodule shared with TPL)
novedades.fuentes: CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG · FIGO · WHO · NICE. · In the Calculator, the single cutoff used is that of MSPBS Paraguay (corticosteroids: 24⁰/⁷ to 34⁰/⁷ weeks, not from 34¹/⁷ onward · MgSO4: less than 32 weeks); ACOG/FIGO/NICE variations are listed in this guide — see Calculator Mode.
novedades.texto: These therapies are shared with the Threatened Preterm Labor (TPL) module — same regimen, same table of recommendations by guideline: Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation (3 recommendations) Guideline GA window ACOG 24⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷ weeks (consider “late preterm” 34⁰/⁷-36⁶/⁷ if no prior course was given) FIGO/WHO 24⁰/⁷-34⁶/⁷ weeks (in settings with adequate neonatal care capacity) NICE Offer 24⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷; consider 34⁰/⁷-35⁶/⁷ Regimens: Betamethasone 12mg IM every 24h (2 doses total); Dexamethasone 6mg IM every 12h (4 doses total). Rescue dose: a single dose or repeat course if >14 days since the initial course, GA<34 weeks, and imminent risk of delivery within 7 days. In PROM, ACOG considers the evidence insufficient for or against a rescue course: it may be considered, without delaying delivery. Fetal neuroprotection with MgSO4 (3 recommendations) Guideline GA cutoff ACOG <32⁰/⁷ weeks NICE <30⁰/⁷ weeks; consider 30⁰/⁷-33⁶/⁷ FIGO/WHO <32⁰/⁷ weeks (some consensus statements extend to <34 weeks if delivery is imminent) CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: ACOG · FIGO · WHO · NICE. Regimen: loading dose 4g IV over 20-30min; maintenance 1g/h IV until delivery or for a total of 24h; antidote: Calcium Gluconate 10% 1g IV. In the Calculator, the single cutoff used is that of MSPBS Paraguay (corticosteroids: 24⁰/⁷ to 34⁰/⁷ weeks, not from 34¹/⁷ onward · MgSO4: less than 32 weeks); ACOG/FIGO/NICE variations are listed in this guide — see Calculator Mode.

Crystallization (Fern test) 55-98% 30-88% Wide range; depends on the operator. IGFBP-1 (Actim PROM) 74-97% 74-97% Commercial alternative to PAMG-1; individual studies show ~89-90% sensitivity and ~83-87% specificity. Vaginal urea (cutoff 1.25 mg/dL) 94% 82% Low cost; useful in resource-limited settings (Alao 2023).
